The handbook is the result of literally thousands of tests of integrated circuits, including the most commonly used digital and linear types.

The susceptibility information is presented in several easy-to-use graphs in Chapter 4, showing the minimum power levels (versus frequency) at which the tested integrated circuits were observed to be susceptible.
Interfering signals at frequencies of 220 MHz, 910 MHz, 3 GHz, 5.6 GHz, and 9.1 GHz were used in the testing.
For a TTL 7400 NAND gate, as little as 9 mW of RF power at 220 MHz was observed to cause logic errors.
For an op amp-based amplifier circuit, output voltage changes were observed with as little as 0.1 mW of 3 GHz RF power conducted into the op amp's inverting input.
The handbook includes information on interference modeling, including the use of SPICE simulations to analyze interference effects in integrated circuits.

The recommended system hardening approach involves determining the electromagnetic environment, calculating pickup levels and component susceptibility, performing a vulnerability assessment, and selecting appropriate hardening techniques.
If the hardening requirement is less than 0 dB, no hardening is needed, but if it is greater than 0 dB, further hardening design or analysis may be required.
The handbook focuses on the frequency range of 100 MHz to 40 GHz, with the upper frequency limit of practical concern closer to 10 GHz.
The handbook notes that there are theoretical and practical considerations that indicate the worst-case problems are adequately covered, even at frequencies below 100 MHz.

The handbook is intended to provide much of the information needed to estimate the susceptibility of circuits containing ICs to RF energy and to approach the hardening task required to ensure operation in high-power RF environments.
The handbook was developed by the McDonnell Douglas Astronautics Company under contract to the U.S. Naval Surface Weapons Center - Dahlgren Laboratory.
Previous drafts of the handbook were widely reviewed, and suggestions and comments received from these versions have been incorporated into this final version.

The handbook is expected to remain a valuable source for many years to come, as the present interference mechanism of rectification is not expected to change with advances in complexity or technology.
The appendix of the handbook describes the equipment and techniques used to measure integrated circuit susceptibilities.
